What I found, once I started cultivating my own happiness, was that I got a lot better at helping other people toward theirs. That might not be how it goes for everyone, and it doesn’t mean unhappy people can’t help. I’d still take real suffering seriously, and do what you owe the people around you, but skip the part where you have to be miserable too.

Some friends or family really might not like it when you get happier, though. Someone might pull away, or keep dragging you back into the old misery. I’d take that loss seriously, and look at what they do and what you owe them, before deciding it’s envy.

If the love still isn’t coming, you can at least stop judging your little one. Obviously no insults. Helpful advice is great, we all need advice. Let them absorb it at their pace. And don’t expect a thank-you for the session, like they booked it. That’s enough to start being the adult, even if it isn’t enough yet for them to trust you. That takes warmth, and if there isn’t any yet, borrow some.

The thank-you you weren’t waiting for might not come anyway. 😜 More like “Oh, so NOW you care?” Your first instinct might be “But I’m trying!” Some days, just hearing it out like a decent adult is the only thing you’ll manage to borrow.

cases.source:
A Belonging Deeper Than Any Group

The Guide also points beyond itself, toward a belonging deeper than any group, one that doesn’t ask you to give up being yourself. That might be nature, or existence itself. It might be whatever your tradition sees as ultimate. Love can come from any of these places, and you also belong there, which is a little different. Maybe you’ve felt that outside somewhere, like you didn’t need anybody’s okay to be there. The way in is time in nature and contemplative practice, like meditation.

With that under you, belonging with people can get a lot less desperate. Not all at once, though. Your little one might still think, “If they stop liking me, I won’t belong anywhere,” and the Guide can remind it there’s more to belong to than them.
